opus-5.5.text:
I think the key is to work backwards from the scenario instead of forwards from the technology. A lot of people in embodied intelligence start by asking, "What's the most general model I can build?" and then go looking for somewhere to use it. My view is that to get something that can actually be replicated at scale, you have to pick a concrete application first and ask what a customer will pay for, every day, without an engineer standing next to the robot.

That forces you to think about the full stack together. It's not just the brain. It's the hardware form factor, the cost of the body, the reliability of the grippers and sensors, the deployment process, the maintenance, and the data loop after deployment. If any one of those breaks, you don't have a product, you have a demo.

On the model side, I've always believed that data is the bottleneck. Real-world teleoperation data is very valuable, but it's expensive and slow to collect. If you rely only on that, it's very hard to reach the scale where generalization really emerges. So our approach has been to lean heavily on synthetic data and simulation: large-scale, physically grounded simulated data for pretraining skills like grasping and navigation, then a relatively small amount of real data to close the sim-to-real gap and adapt to the specific scenario. That changes the economics. You're no longer paying for every single trajectory with human hours.

Then there's the question of how general to be. I don't think the first scalable products will be a humanoid that can do everything in your home. They'll be in semi-structured environments like retail, pharmacies, warehouses, and factory material handling, where the set of tasks is bounded but the objects and layouts vary a lot. That's exactly where learned generalization beats traditional automation. A traditional system has to be re-engineered for every new SKU or shelf layout. A model that has learned to grasp tens of thousands of objects in simulation can just handle it.

So my answer is to choose a vertical where generalization creates real value, design the hardware to be good enough and cheap enough, use simulation and synthetic data to get the foundational skills, and get robots deployed so real-world feedback flows back into training. Once one scenario works end to end and you can copy it to the hundredth store with almost no extra customization, that's when you've really built a solution, and that template is what lets you expand to the next scenario.

r001.rationale: It recommends choosing a concrete application first, designing around its requirements, and deploying a solution that can be copied at scale.

r002.rationale: It says scalable products can target environments where “the set of tasks is bounded,” rather than requiring a robot that can do everything.

r003.rationale: It contrasts bounded tasks with variation in objects and layouts, explaining that learned skills such as grasping can generalize across many objects and layouts.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about what "complete solution" actually means, because people use that phrase very loosely. A demo is not a solution. A robot that can pick ten objects in a lab under controlled lighting is not a solution. A complete solution is something that runs in a real customer's environment, handles the full distribution of situations that environment throws at it, meets a success rate the customer will actually pay for, and does that across many sites without a PhD standing next to it. If you hold yourself to that definition, a lot of what looks like progress in this field falls away, and what remains is the real work.

So how do you get there? I would break it into three layers, and all three have to be solved together.

The first layer is the model, and specifically generalization. The reason embodied intelligence has historically not scaled is that every deployment was effectively a new engineering project. You tune for one warehouse, one shelf, one lighting condition, and then you move to the next site and you start over. That cost structure makes replication impossible. So the core question for me has always been: can the model generalize to objects, scenes, and layouts it has never seen? Our approach has been to lean very heavily on synthetic data and simulation. We can generate tens of millions, hundreds of millions of grasping and manipulation instances with full physics, full diversity of objects and clutter, and train a foundation model that already has a strong prior before it ever touches a real robot. Then you use a comparatively small amount of real data to close the sim-to-real gap. If you try to do this with real data only, you simply cannot afford the diversity you need, and diversity is what gives you generalization. Generalization is what gives you replicability.

The second layer is the hardware and the system integration, and I think many AI people underestimate this. A model that works does not mean a product that works. You need the arm, the hand, the mobile base, the sensors, the compute, the safety systems, all co-designed around the task so that the whole thing is reliable and cheap enough. Reliability is not glamorous but it is everything. If the system is 95 percent reliable, the customer needs a human to cover the other 5 percent, and then you have not actually removed the human, you have just given them a more complicated job. You need to get to a point where failures are rare, recoverable, and don't require someone with deep expertise to intervene. That is as much a mechanical and systems engineering problem as an AI problem.

The third layer is choosing the scenario correctly. I'm quite opinionated about this. If you pick a scenario that is too open-ended, say a general household robot, you will be fighting the long tail forever and you will not reach a commercial threshold. If you pick a scenario that is too narrow, you are just building a specialized automation machine and the "intelligence" part adds no value. The sweet spot is a scenario that is structured enough to be achievable with today's models, but has enough variation that generalization genuinely matters and a traditional automation approach cannot cover it. That is why we chose things like pharmacy retail, where the physical layout is semi-structured, the task is clear, but the object set is large and keeps changing, and there are thousands of nearly identical stores. Nearly identical sites with a lot of object variation is exactly the profile where a generalizable model plus a standard hardware platform gives you a solution that copies.

And then there is a flywheel that only turns once you have real deployments. Every store you deploy to gives you data on real failure modes, which goes back into the simulation and the training pipeline, which improves the model, which makes the next deployment easier. The value of the first ten deployments is mostly not the revenue, it is the fact that they turn you from a lab into a company with a closed loop. But you only get that loop if the first deployments are good enough that the customer keeps the robot running. So it comes back to reliability again.

If I had to summarize: build for generalization from the start so you are not re-engineering every site, treat the whole robot as the product rather than the model as the product, pick a scenario where the variation is in the objects rather than in the environment, and get real systems into the field as early as you responsibly can so the data loop closes. Those four things together are what I would call a replicable solution. Without any one of them, you have a very impressive demo.

r001.rationale: It frames development around a real customer application that must meet its requirements and replicate across many sites, including choosing a suitable scenario and designing the full system for it.

r002.rationale: It discusses grasping and manipulation but does not state that a limited repertoire of action skills can suffice for a complete application solution.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes generalization across objects, scenes, and layouts, but does not distinguish the breadth of action skills from generalization within those skills.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point has to be a specific application. Who is the customer, what task do they need done, and what would make a robot useful enough that they would pay for it? If we start with a general-purpose robot and then look for somewhere to put it, we can spend a long time demonstrating capabilities without arriving at a complete solution.

Once we choose an application, we need to close the whole loop. That includes the hardware, perception, decision-making, control, and integration with the customer’s workflow. It also includes things that are less exciting in a demonstration: how the robot recovers from a failed grasp, when it asks for help, how it is maintained, and how much human intervention it requires. The customer is buying a result, so all of those things affect whether the solution works.

Then we need to distinguish between making it work at one site and making it replicable. If every new deployment requires a team of engineers to redesign the system, that is still a custom project. We should identify what stays consistent across customers and keep the amount of site-specific adaptation small. The task should be sufficiently bounded that we can measure reliability, throughput, and cost under real operating conditions.

Deployment also needs to generate useful feedback. Failures in the field should feed into data collection, training, and testing, so that solving a problem at one site improves the system at other sites. That is how deployment can become progressively easier rather than simply adding more engineering work.

So I would start with a narrow but valuable task, build a complete operational loop, and prove that the economics and reliability hold across multiple sites. From there, we can expand the range of tasks. Generality is valuable, but it needs to translate into something concrete: less adaptation, fewer interventions, and a lower cost of delivering the result.

r001.rationale: It recommends starting with a specific, bounded application and proving reliability and economics across multiple sites so the solution can be replicated at scale.

r002.rationale: It advocates a narrow task, but does not state that a limited repertoire of action skills is enough for a complete application solution.

r003.rationale: It discusses generality as reducing adaptation and intervention, but does not distinguish the breadth of action skills from how broadly those skills generalize.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to start with a clearly defined application. What task does the robot need to perform, in what environment, and what level of reliability and cost would make it useful? Without those constraints, it is easy to build an impressive demonstration that is difficult to turn into a product.

Then we need to develop the whole system together: the hardware, perception, decision-making, control, and the way people interact with it. A stronger model alone does not necessarily produce a better solution. The robot has to complete the task consistently, recognize when it cannot, and recover or ask for help.

The next step is to close the loop between deployment and improvement. Real operation reveals failures that you won’t anticipate in the lab. We need a way to collect those cases, improve the system, and verify that the improvement works across different sites rather than only fixing one particular situation.

For replication at scale, I would distinguish between a common platform and the adaptation required for each customer. If every deployment requires extensive engineering from scratch, it is still a custom project. The goal is to make deployment, calibration, maintenance, and training increasingly standardized.

So I would start with a relatively bounded task, make the complete solution reliable and economically useful, and then expand its capabilities. The measure of progress is whether you can deliver the same value repeatedly, with less effort each time.

r001.rationale: It centers development on a clearly defined, bounded application and explains how to standardize deployment so the solution can be replicated at scale.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with a bounded task, but does not state that a limited repertoire of action skills can suffice for a complete solution.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish the breadth of action skills from the breadth of generalization within those skills.
